summary: Provides typical call-flow examples for the Media Control Channel Framework, a guide to the interface between application servers and media servers, useful for implementers and protocol researchers. The examples are informational and define no new protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Step-by-step examples show how a boss program asks a helper machine to play sounds and run calls.

questions: how does an application server control a media server
what is mediactrl and how is it used
how are multimedia services like conferencing and voicemail implemented
subtitle: Practical examples of how application servers control media servers using the MEDIACTRL framework.

tldr.problem: The Media Control Channel Framework (MEDIACTRL) provides a way for application servers to control media servers, but the abstract protocol specification is hard to apply to real-world scenarios. Implementers needed practical examples of how to set up connections, run call flows, and handle common use cases.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides detailed call flow examples showing how application servers and media servers interact using MEDIACTRL messages (CONTROL, SYNC, K-ALIVE) to establish control channels, handle media operations like conferencing and IVR, and manage security boundaries between different clients.
tldr.outcome: The document became an essential reference for developers building MEDIACTRL implementations, showing how the framework enables rich multimedia services like conferences, voice mail, call recording, and DTMF-controlled features.

today: RFC 7058 remains an essential reference for anyone implementing MEDIACTRL-based media servers or application servers. While it is an Informational document that does not define new protocol extensions, it has become the de facto guide to understanding how to use the framework in practice. The MEDIACTRL suite itself (RFC 6230, 6231, 6505, 6917) remains active and in use in VoIP systems, though adoption has been slower than anticipated due to competition from simpler approaches.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
This RFC provides a guide to the MEDIACTRL framework by presenting detailed call flow examples. MEDIACTRL is the mechanism by which an Application Server (AS) requests media processing from a Media Server (MS), such as mixing audio for conferences, playing announcements, recording calls, or collecting DTMF keypad input.

The RFC focuses on practical scenarios based on implementation experience with the framework. It covers the interaction between a single AS and a single MS, though it also includes examples involving a Media Resource Broker that helps multiple AS instances find suitable MS resources.

The document is not meant to replace the core MEDIACTRL specifications (RFC 6230, 6231, 6505, and 6917); instead, it complements them by showing how the framework is actually used in real-world multimedia applications.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a guide showing step-by-step examples of how a program that runs a phone service talks to the helper machine that actually plays sounds and records voices.

sections.title: State Diagrams and Protocol States
sections.content:
Before diving into specific scenarios, the RFC presents state diagrams that model how the framework operates. These diagrams use a Mealy automaton approach, showing the states each entity goes through during a transaction and the inputs and outputs that trigger state transitions.

The Media Server state diagram shows that the MS listens for CONTROL messages from the AS. When a command is quick to execute, the MS replies with a 200 message immediately. When the command takes time, the MS first sends a 202 response (with a timeout value) and transitions to a '202' sent state. While in that state, the MS periodically sends REPORT update messages. Finally, it sends a REPORT terminate message when done.

The Application Server state diagram mirrors the MS behavior: it sends CONTROL messages, receives responses, and acknowledges any REPORT messages. A separate diagram shows how event notifications work, where the MS sends CONTROL messages to the AS to report asynchronous events (like DTMF digits or voice detection).
sections.plainLanguage: The diagrams show the steps both the boss and helper go through: the boss asks for work, the helper either finishes quickly or says it will take a moment and then gives updates, and finally it says it is done.

sections.title: Establishing the Control Channel
sections.content:
Before any media service request can be made, the AS and MS must establish a Control Channel between them - a reliable TCP or SCTP connection.

The establishment process has three main steps: First, the AS and MS use COMEDIA (connection-oriented media) negotiation via SIP. The AS sends an INVITE message with an SDP body containing a cfw-id attribute (a globally unique dialog identifier) and specifying the port it will listen on. The MS responds with its own port and confirms the same cfw-id. Second, the AS connects to the MS using the negotiated address and port. Third, the AS sends a SYNC message on the TCP connection, including the cfw-id to validate that the connection came from the expected peer. The SYNC message also negotiates which Control Packages the MS should activate (like msc-mixer/1.0 for conferencing or msc-ivr/1.0 for IVR) and the keep-alive timeout (typically 100 seconds).

The RFC also covers common mistakes during setup, such as sending a CONTROL message instead of SYNC as the first transaction, or using the wrong Dialog-ID in the SYNC message. In such cases, the MS rejects the connection with a 403 (Forbidden) or 481 (Call/Transaction Does Not Exist) error.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss and helper first agree on how they will talk (using a phone call setup), then the boss connects to the helper, and then the boss sends a special message that proves who it is. They also agree on a keep-alive signal to make sure the connection stays open.

sections.title: Keep-Alive and Connection Management
sections.content:
The MEDIACTRL framework includes a keep-alive mechanism to maintain the Control Channel when NATs or firewalls might otherwise close idle connections. The AS and MS negotiate a keep-alive timeout during the SYNC exchange. The specification suggests that the active endpoint (typically the AS) should send a K-ALIVE message when approximately 80% of the timeout interval has elapsed. If no activity occurs before the full timeout expires, the connection is torn down.

In the example provided, with a 100-second timeout, the AS sends a K-ALIVE message at about 80 seconds, the MS acknowledges it with a 200 response, and both reset their local timers. This cycle repeats indefinitely as long as the connection is needed. The RFC also notes that applications can send actual media control requests instead of K-ALIVE messages to satisfy the keep-alive requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: If the boss and helper are not talking for a while, one of them periodically sends a short message saying "I am still here" to keep the connection from being closed by a firewall.

sections.title: Practical Use-Case Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC presents a comprehensive set of real-world scenarios that the MEDIACTRL framework enables. The Echo Test is the simplest: a user can test their connection by speaking and hearing themselves echoed back. This is implemented by joining a connection to itself.

The Phone Call scenario covers direct connections between users, as well as a conference-based approach where participants connect through a mixer. The RFC also shows how to record conversations.

The Conferencing scenarios are the most elaborate. Simple bridging joins participants to a conference so they can hear a mix of all speakers. Rich conference scenarios add IVR menus for PIN entry, announcements when people join, and name recording. The Coaching scenario is particularly detailed: a customer, an agent, and a coach all participate, but the customer can only hear the agent, the agent hears both the customer and the coach (who whispers with reduced volume), and the coach hears everyone. This is achieved by creating a hidden conference with specific mixing policies for each participant, then joining the customer directly to the agent for a primary audio path.

The RFC also covers sidebars (sub-conferences within a larger conference), floor control to manage who can speak, voice mail systems, and DTMF-driven conference manipulation (e.g., unmuting participants via keypad entry).
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how the framework handles simple things like echoing your voice, connecting two calls, and complex things like conferences where different people hear different things, all controlled by the helper machine at the direction of the boss program.

sections.title: Media Resource Brokering
sections.content:
When multiple Application Servers need media services, they may use a Media Resource Broker to locate and reserve suitable Media Servers. This broker acts as a registry and matchmaker.

The RFC describes the broker's dual interface: the Publishing Interface allows MS instances to advertise their capabilities (such as supported packages, codecs, and capacity). The Consumer Interface allows AS instances to query available resources or request reservations. The RFC covers three consumer modes: Query Mode (the AS asks what resources are available), Inline-Aware Mode (the broker reserves resources on behalf of the AS), and Inline-Unaware Mode (the AS reserves resources but relies on the broker for media dialog handling).

The call flows show how an AS can discover a suitable MS, how the broker handles media dialogs across different endpoints, and how the CFW protocol behavior adapts to the brokering architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: When there are many helper machines, a coordinator program (the broker) keeps track of which ones are available and helps the boss program pick one that can do the job.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that because the Control Channel gives direct access to powerful media resources (conferences, recordings, dialogs), security is critical. The MS must prevent one AS from manipulating resources created by another AS.

The RFC demonstrates this with a detailed scenario where two Application Servers (AS1 and AS2) have separate Control Channels with the same MS. When AS1 sends an audit request to list all active conferences and dialogs, the MS returns only the resources created by AS1, not those of AS2, even though the MS knows about both. Similarly, when AS1 tries to terminate a dialog created by AS2, the MS rejects the request with a 403 (Forbidden) error.

The Dialog-ID, negotiated during the SYNC phase, allows the MS to bind each Control Channel to a specific AS context. Resources created within that context are isolated: their identifiers are not revealed in audit responses to other AS instances, and operations on those identifiers from unauthorized AS instances are denied. This ensures that the MS acts as a trusted arbiter of resource access.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper machine makes sure that if two different boss programs are both using it, each one can only see and control its own work, not the other one's.

sections.title: Key Implementation Insights
sections.content:
Throughout the RFC, several practical insights emerge for implementers. The use of SIP tags (the From and To tags of the Control Channel SIP dialog) concatenated with media labels (assigned via SDP) allows the AS and MS to uniquely identify all participants and media streams in a session. This three-tier addressing scheme - Dialog-ID for the control channel, Connection ID (tags) for media sessions, and Label for individual media streams - enables fine-grained control over complex scenarios.

The RFC also clarifies the difference between messages that execute quickly (receiving a 200 response immediately) and long-running operations (receiving a 202 response followed by periodic REPORT updates). The Timeout header in responses tells the AS how long to wait before timing out a pending operation.

Transaction correlation is handled via a transaction ID included in every request and response, allowing the AS to match replies to requests even in the presence of out-of-order messages. The examples show proper error handling, including how error codes signal different failure modes (481 for invalid dialog, 403 for unauthorized access, etc.).
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show practical tricks for tracking who is who, handling work that takes a long time, and knowing when something goes wrong.

viz.caption: Core Multimedia Services Enabled by MEDIACTRL

items.title: Conferencing
items.text: Mix audio and video from multiple participants, apply layout policies, control floor and sidebars.

items.title: IVR (Interactive Voice Response)
items.text: Collect DTMF input, play announcements and prompts, record user responses.

items.title: Call Recording
items.text: Capture media from calls for compliance, quality assurance, or playback.

items.title: Media Mixing
items.text: Join participants with specific direction policies (sendonly, recvonly, sendrecv) and per-participant mix preferences.

items.title: Resource Brokering
items.text: Discover and reserve media servers via a broker when multiple servers are available.

items.title: Real-Time Media Control
items.text: Dynamically mute/unmute, change video layouts, adjust volume gains, and handle floor control during calls.
